problem: The Bash scripts (Session 105) and Python automation (Session 106) you now write need a home that survives you: change history, rollback, code review, and safe collaboration across a team without emailing files around or overwriting each other's work. Without version control, “which version of the deploy script is actually running in production” becomes unanswerable, and a single bad edit can't be traced or undone.

Git solves this by tracking every change to every file over time, enabling multiple engineers to work on the same automation codebase in parallel, and providing the audit trail that enterprise change- management and compliance processes require.

Why it matters here: Every tool in this layer from this point forward — Infrastructure as Code, Configuration Management, CI/CD — assumes its definitions (Terraform files, Ansible playbooks, pipeline YAML) live in Git. Git is not optional infrastructure; it is the substrate everything else in Automation is built on.
concept: Git is a distributed version control system: every clone of a repository is a full copy of the entire history, not just a checkout of the current state. This is fundamentally different from older centralized systems (SVN, CVS) where history lived only on a central server.
A repository is a graph of commits — immutable snapshots, each pointing to its parent(s).
A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit — lightweight, cheap to create, meant to be created constantly.
The working directory, staging area (index), and repository (.git) are three distinct states a file passes through before a change is permanently recorded.

Distributed-by-design is what makes Git the natural fit for infrastructure-as-code: every engineer, and every CI runner, can have a complete, independent copy of the automation history, with no single point of failure.
deep: The Three Trees three-trees Working Directory --git add--> Staging Area (Index) --git commit--> Repository (.git) Everyday Workflow basic-workflow git status git add fleet-health-check.sh git commit -m "Add fleet health check script" git log --oneline --graph --all git push origin main Branching and Merging branching git checkout -b feature/add-slack-alert git add . && git commit -m "Add Slack alerting" git checkout main git merge feature/add-slack-alert git branch -d feature/add-slack-alert
Fast-forward merge — target branch has no new commits since the feature branch diverged; the pointer simply moves forward.
Three-way merge — both branches diverged; Git creates a new merge commit with two parents.
Rebase — replays your branch's commits on top of another branch, producing linear history instead of a merge commit: git rebase main.

Conflict Resolution merge-conflict-markers <<<<<<< HEAD THRESHOLD=80 THRESHOLD=90 >>>>>>> feature/tune-threshold A conflict happens when Git cannot automatically reconcile two changes to the same lines; you edit the file to the correct final content, remove the markers, `git add` the file, then complete the commit or rebase.

Undoing Things undo-operations git restore --staged file.sh # unstage, keep working-dir changes git checkout -- file.sh # discard working-dir changes (legacy syntax) git revert <commit> # new commit that undoes an old one (safe on shared history) git reset --hard <commit> # rewrite branch pointer, discard changes (danger on shared history) Golden rule: Never `reset --hard` or force-push on a branch other people have already pulled — use `revert` on shared/public history, reserve `reset` for your own local, unpushed commits.
Remotes remotes git remote add origin git@github.com:org/infra-automation.git git fetch origin git pull origin main git push -u origin feature/add-slack-alert
workflow: Understanding Git's internal object model explains why operations that look scary (rebase, reset) are actually safe and recoverable.
1. Blob — Git stores file *content* as a blob, addressed by the SHA-1 (or SHA-256 in newer repos) hash of its contents, not its filename.
2. Tree — a tree object represents a directory: a list of blobs and other trees, each with a filename and mode.
3. Commit — points to exactly one tree (the full snapshot of the repo at that point) plus parent commit(s), author, committer, and message.
4. Refs — a branch is a file containing a commit SHA; HEAD is a pointer to the current branch (or a specific commit, in detached-HEAD state).
5. `git add` hashes file content into a blob and stages it in the index; `git commit` writes a new tree from the index and a new commit object pointing to it.

6. `git push` transfers any objects the remote doesn't already have (content-addressed, so it's efficient) and updates the remote's ref/branch pointer — this is why push can be rejected (non-fast-forward) if the remote has commits you don't.
enterprise: Source of truth for Infrastructure as Code (Session 109) — Terraform state definitions, module code, and variable files live in Git, often with mandatory pull-request review before terraform apply.
Configuration Management (Session 110) — Ansible playbooks and roles are versioned in Git;
changes are peer-reviewed the same way application code is.

CI/CD (Session 111) — pipelines are triggered by Git events (push, tag, pull-request merge); the pipeline definition itself (.gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, GitHub Actions workflow) is also stored in Git alongside the code it builds.

GitOps — an increasingly standard enterprise pattern where the desired state of production infrastructure is declared entirely in a Git repository, and an operator continuously reconciles the live environment to match it.
Change management / audit / compliance — Git's commit history (who changed what, when, and why via commit messages) satisfies audit requirements that manual change tickets used to handle manually.
dependencies: Dependency Why Git needs it File Systems (Layer 2) The .git directory is itself a structured set of files (objects, refs, config) on the local filesystem.
Networking (Layer 3) Push/pull/fetch/clone over HTTPS or SSH depend on TCP/IP and TLS.
Identity (Layer 4) SSH keys or OAuth tokens authenticate pushes to remote repos (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket, or an internal Git server).
Bash (Session 105) Git hooks default to shell scripts; many Git workflows are wrapped in Bash tooling.
dependents: REST APIs (Session 108) — GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket expose REST (and GraphQL) APIs to automate repository management, which many CI/CD and ChatOps tools consume directly.
Infrastructure as Code (Session 109) — Terraform's whole workflow (plan/apply, module versioning, state review) assumes code lives in Git.
Configuration Management (Session 110) — Ansible roles are commonly distributed via Git repos (including via Ansible Galaxy, itself Git-backed).
CI/CD (Session 111) — the entire discipline is built around Git events as triggers and Git history as the deployment record.

Secrets Management (Session 112) — precisely because Git preserves full history forever, secrets accidentally committed must be rotated, not just deleted — a security consequence covered in Section 8 below.
security: Secrets committed to Git never truly disappear — even after deleting a file and committing again, the secret remains in history and any prior clone. The only safe remediation is rotating the credential *and* rewriting history (git filter-repo / BFG) if the repo is not yet fully public.
SSH key vs HTTPS token auth — SSH deploy keys and personal access tokens should be scoped to the minimum required repositories/permissions, not account-wide admin tokens.
Signed commits (git commit -S, GPG or SSH signing) let you verify a commit truly came from the claimed author, important for supply-chain integrity on infrastructure repos.

Branch protection rules — require pull-request review and passing CI checks before merging to main, preventing a single compromised or careless credential from pushing directly to production- facing code.

`.gitignore` discipline — keep credentials, .env files, and state files with secrets (e.g., Terraform state containing plaintext secrets) out of the repository from the start; a pre-commit hook scanning for secret patterns is a common enterprise safeguard.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause Fix "failed to push, non-fast-forward" Remote has commits you don't have locally `git pull --rebase origin main` then push again Merge conflict markers left in a file after resolving Forgot to remove `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>> >` before committing Edit the file to final content, remove markers, `git add`, continue merge/rebase Accidentally committed to `main` instead of a feature branch Forgot to create/checkout a branch first `git branch feature/x` then `git reset --hard origin/main` on main (only if unpushed) or cherry-pick the commit onto the new branch "detached HEAD" warning after checking out a commit SHA Checked out a commit directly instead of a branch `git checkout -b new-branch- name` to attach a branch pointer to that commit before making changes Large binary accidentally committed, repo size ballooning Binary/artifact committed instead of ignored Add to `.gitignore` going forward;
use `git filter-repo` to purge it from history if needed

repo-layout infra-automation/ scripts/ fleet-health-check.sh check_inventory.py ansible/ playbooks/ terraform/ modules/ .github/workflows/ci.yml .gitignore README.md A typical pull-request workflow: an engineer branches off `main`, edits `fleet-health-check.sh` to add a new alert threshold, opens a pull request, CI automatically lints and syntax-checks the script (tying back to `shellcheck` from Session 105), a teammate reviews and approves, and merging to `main` automatically triggers a CI/CD deployment (Session 111) of the updated script to production hosts.
cloud: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket are the dominant hosted Git platforms; each adds pull/merge requests, CI/CD runners, issue tracking, and access control on top of core Git.

AWS CodeCommit, Azure Repos, and Google Cloud Source Repositories offer cloud-native, IAM-integrated Git hosting inside each provider's ecosystem — useful when repo access needs to align tightly with existing cloud IAM roles.

GitOps operators (Argo CD, Flux) watch a Git repository and continuously reconcile a Kubernetes cluster's actual state to match what's declared in Git — Git becomes the deployment mechanism itself, not just a code store.
Cloud-native CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, AWS CodePipeline) is triggered directly by Git webhooks, tightly coupling every push to an automated build/test/deploy cycle.
automation: Git's role in the automation stack is as the **system of record**: every other tool in this layer reads its configuration, code, or desired state from a Git repository, and many write their execution history back as commits or tags.

Tool What it stores in Git Bash / Python (Sessions 105–106) The scripts themselves, with full change history Terraform (Session 109) HCL definitions, modules, sometimes remote state locking references Ansible (Session 110) Playbooks, roles, inventory files CI/CD (Session 111) Pipeline-as-code definitions (Jenkinsfile, .gitlab- ci.yml, workflow YAML)
career: Git fluency is assumed, not optional, for essentially every technical role — DevOps, SRE, developer, data engineer — making it one of the highest-leverage skills in this entire curriculum relative to effort invested.
Interviewers frequently probe beyond basic add/commit/push: rebase vs merge trade-offs, resolving conflicts, and recovering from a bad reset separate intermediate from senior candidates.
Understanding GitOps is increasingly a differentiator for Platform Engineer and SRE roles as Kubernetes-based, Git-driven deployment models become standard.
Being the person on a team who can calmly fix a broken rebase or recover a “lost” commit via git reflog builds outsized trust relative to the actual difficulty of the skill.

misconceptions: “Git and GitHub are the same thing.” Git is the version control system; GitHub is one of several hosted platforms built around it (alongside GitLab, Bitbucket, self-hosted Gitea) — Git itself works fully offline with no GitHub account at all.
“Deleting a file removes it from history.” It only removes it from the latest snapshot; every prior commit, and anyone who cloned before the deletion, still has it.
“Rebase rewrites the original commits.” Rebase creates brand-new commits with new SHAs that replay the same changes; the originals still exist (recoverable via reflog) until garbage-collected.

“`git pull` is a single atomic safe operation.” git pull is fetch + merge (or rebase if configured) — it can produce merge conflicts you weren't expecting if you don't understand what it's doing underneath.
anchors: “Branches are pointers, not folders” — creating one is nearly free; use them liberally.
“A secret in history is a secret forever” — until rotated, deleting the file changes nothing.
“Revert on shared history, reset on your own” — the golden rule for not breaking a teammate's clone.
“Git is content-addressed” — every object is identified by the hash of its content, which is why push/fetch only transfer what's actually new.
